title: Review: 4-hour Musk documentary feels like two different films
gist: Jennifer Ouellette reviews Alex Gibney's nearly four-hour documentary Musk, which portrays Elon Musk as a Gilded Age-style confidence man and stock promoter, but feels like two separate films split around the Twitter purchase and Trump embrace. She finds it compelling but incomplete in explaining why Musk ended up on a dark path.

insights.claim: Gibney's documentary Musk presents Elon Musk as a Gilded Age confidence man updated for the 21st century, an investor posing as an inventor whose real talent is pumping stocks and dazzling investors and the public with high-tech utopian visions.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Frames Musk's valuation-driving narrative as showmanship, which is the reputational lens a mainstream film will push into public perception of his companies.
insights.quote: an investor cosplaying as an inventor whose real genius is pumping stocks and dazzling investors and the public alike
insights.locator: Gibney’s documentary presents Musk as more of a Gilded Age

insights.claim: The film also frames Musk as a tragic anti-hero, an idealistic dreamer corrupted by wealth and power, which Gibney calls noble cause corruption, though it sheds little light on why he ended up on a dark path.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The film's explanatory gap means it is unlikely to shift views beyond existing priors.
insights.locator: Musk is a frequently compelling portrait

insights.claim: The reviewer argues Musk's detachment from reality has grown with his wealth and influence, and that an interview probably would not have helped because he cannot engage in self-reflection and can keep his bubble intact.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Reviewer opinion; suggests key-person and governance risk perceptions around Musk are entrenched.
insights.locator: Would Musk agreeing to be interviewed have helped

themes.theme: Film structure: two films in one

insights.claim: The documentary feels like two films: a first half on Musk's early entrepreneurial years using archival footage, and a markedly more adversarial second half after his Twitter purchase and embrace of Trump.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Marks the Twitter acquisition and political turn as the inflection point in how Musk is portrayed.
insights.locator: But the documentary ends up feeling like two very different films

insights.claim: Gibney finished the film in 2024 but HBO asked him to continue to document Musk's heel turn, which likely explains the split and the runtime ballooning to nearly four hours with a 10-minute intermission; Gibney joked it could have run six hours.
insights.speaker: Alex Gibney
insights.so_what: Shows how recent Musk events reshaped the project; minor for investors beyond narrative context.
insights.locator: During a post-screening Q&A, Gibney revealed

insights.claim: The film covers Tesla and fatalities linked to its driver-assistance systems, SpaceX, Starlink, the Twitter purchase, his shift from warning about AI risks to embracing it with Grok, his embrace of Trump, DOGE creation, alleged drug use and his 14 or more children.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Lists the reputational and regulatory threads attached to Musk-linked companies that could feature in public discourse.
insights.locator: There’s certainly no shortage of material for Gibney

insights.claim: Interviewees include Justine Musk, Kara Swisher, Martin Eberhard, Geoffrey Hinton, Ashley St. Clair, Cory Doctorow, Adam Becker and Sam Harris, with David Byrne co-writing the song Let Me Sell You a Dream.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Context on the film's sourcing breadth, including early Tesla insider Eberhard and AI figure Hinton.
insights.locator: Those interviewed include ex-wife Justine Musk

insights.claim: Before release the film drew Musk's ire and threats of a defamation lawsuit, plus unfounded rumors that Universal Pictures was getting cold feet about international theatrical release; Musk has called it a hit piece, which the reviewer disputes.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Litigation or distribution friction is possible but unsubstantiated; low direct market relevance.
insights.locator: Gibney has never been one to shy away from controversy

insights.claim: Musk is in select theaters in New York and Los Angeles and opens nationwide on October 14.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Wide release date is a near-term catalyst for renewed Musk media attention.
insights.locator: Musk is now playing in select theaters

insights.claim: Because Musk declined to be interviewed, Gibney created an AI version of him speaking verbatim public quotes; the reviewer finds it conceptually apt but executed as creepy uncanny valley, far less interesting than real archival footage.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Documentary use of synthetic stand-ins is a mainstream normalization of AI avatars with mixed reception.
insights.locator: Musk declined to be interviewed for the film
